Holocaust. The systematic, state-sponsored genocide of six million Jews perpetrated by Nazi Germany and its collaborators between nineteen-thirty-three and nineteen-forty-five, along with the murder of millions of others: Roma, disabled people, political prisoners, homosexuals, and others deemed racially or socially undesirable. It represents the most comprehensive and industrialized genocide in human history, a crime of unprecedented scale that fundamentally altered understanding of human capacity for evil. The Holocaust stands as a defining atrocity of modernity and a warning against ideology, totalitarianism, and unchecked state violence.

The Holocaust began with antisemitic laws and exclusions after Hitler's rise to power in nineteen-thirty-three, progressively stripping Jews of citizenship, property, and rights. It escalated during World War Two with forced ghettoization of European Jews, particularly in Poland, where millions were concentrated in horrific conditions.

The genocide transformed into systematic extermination after the invasion of the Soviet Union in nineteen-forty-one through mobile killing squads called Einsatzgruppen and fixed death camps constructed specifically for mass murder. These camps, including Auschwitz-Birkenau, Treblinka, and Sobibor, used poison gas, starvation, disease, and brutal forced labor to murder millions. The system depended on administrative infrastructure, railroad transport, and extensive collaboration from local populations across occupied Europe, demonstrating how genocide required systematic organization.

The Holocaust killed approximately six million Jews, along with three million Roma, two million disabled people, Soviet prisoners of war, and political and religious dissidents. It remained systematically concealed from world knowledge until liberation by Allied forces in nineteen-forty-four and nineteen-forty-five, after which survivors provided testimony crucial to understanding the genocide.
